The newly emerged yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], reflecting the minute egg diameter typical of the genus. This early developmental phase is brief and energetically demanding, as the lecithotrophic larvae must quickly absorb their endogenous yolk reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. As individuals progress through the juvenile phase and approach sexual maturation, their somatic growth follows a predictable trajectory. Corresponding to this ultimate length, the maximum wet weight achieved by mature individuals is 268 grams [Wwi = 268 grams], a moderately large body mass for a malacanthid fish. These size thresholds appear to be tightly linked to the onset of reproductive competence, as gravid females are rarely encountered below this mass. The incubation period at this temperature is notably brief, with embryos completing development and hatching after only 8 days. This rapid embryonic development is advantageous in the warm, food-rich waters of the subtropical shelf, reducing the window of vulnerability for the pelagic egg stage. The hatchlings emerge at a wet weight of just 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], a mass that underscores their extreme altriciality at the moment of chorion rupture and the subsequent dependence on planktonic prey availability during the early larval phase.

The combination of slow somatic growth after maturity and a prolonged reproductive window suggests that B. argentatus follows a relatively conservative life-history strategy, prioritizing adult survival and repeated reproductive bouts over a single, high-investment spawning event.
